q: Vineyards were sorted into first, second and third class in a Hungarian region during the eighteenth century, generations before any French list did the same. Which region?
exp: The survey graded the ground rather than the producers, and it was made for a crown that wanted to protect and to tax a valuable export. Its classes were carried into the region's later rules, which is why it is usually cited as the earliest vineyard classification still recognisable in its modern form.

q: Four phrases turn up across a shelf of European bottles: Grand Cru Classe, Vieilles Vignes, Riserva and Cuvee. Which pair may anybody print without meeting any rule at all?
exp: Grand Cru Classe and Riserva are protected terms with rulebooks and inspectors behind them, and the other two are the producer's own prose: cuvee means a vatful, and old vines means whatever the estate thinks old is. The habit worth building is to sort every word on a label into those two piles before saying anything about the wine.

q: Two Spanish denominations have been promoted to the rung above DO in more than thirty years of the system, one writing the extra word in Castilian and the other in Catalan. Name them.
exp: Rioja took the qualified rank first and Priorat followed a decade later, and nothing has joined them since, which is a fair measure of how rarely the top rung opens. The requirements reach past the wine into how the denomination polices its own members, so the promotion is as much about the body as about the bottles.

q: Leaving a Spanish denomination, every bottle carries a numbered label on its back, issued by the regulating body and counted against what the bodega declared. Name it.
exp: Issuing the seals in a fixed quantity is how a denomination polices volume, because the number handed out cannot exceed what the registered vineyard could lawfully have produced. It also carries the ageing tier, so the claim on the front is matched by a strip on the back that the body itself printed. A plain etiqueta is any label at all, and it is the contra that makes this one the regulator's.

q: Nothing in wine law stands behind a private ranking, and yet its owner can stop an outsider printing the same words. Which body of law does that work?
exp: A ranking that is not a law is a name, and a name is protected by registering it, which is why private schemes register their words and their emblems and go to court as brand owners rather than as appellations. It also shapes how they behave: an owner who tolerates a copy risks the mark going generic, so a private scheme has to police its words far more visibly than a state body ever does.

q: Caught breaking the rules attached to a private association's top rank, a member faces the only real sanction such a body holds. What is it?
exp: A private scheme cannot fine anybody and has no inspectorate with a statutory footing, so its whole leverage is the right to use the mark and the company of the other members. That is why such schemes are often stricter than the law on paper and slower than the law in practice, since throwing out a famous name is a public act with consequences in both directions.

q: Name the two broad strategies for pairing, one matching like with like and the other setting them against each other.
exp: Complement echoes a quality the dish already has; contrast supplies what it lacks. Most classic pairings are one or the other stated plainly.

q: Before any question of flavour, which single structural quality should be matched between dish and wine?
exp: A delicate wine disappears under a heavy dish and a heavy wine flattens a delicate one. Weight is the first filter and it settles most bad pairings before flavour is considered.

q: A dish's sweetness sets a floor for the wine. What follows from that?
opts: The wine must be at least as sweet
The wine should be drier, to cut the dish's sweetness
A high-acid dry wine will balance the sweetness
Sweetness in food has no bearing on the pairing
exp: Sweeter food strips a wine of fruit and leaves acid and alcohol exposed. Matching or exceeding the dish's sweetness is the one near-inviolable rule of dessert pairing, and acidity is no substitute for it: a dry high-acid wine set against a sweet dish is left tasting sour rather than refreshing.

q: A dish high in acidity demands what of the wine, if the wine is not to taste flat?
exp: Acid in the dish resets the palate and makes a lower-acid wine taste dull and flabby. Meeting it keeps the wine tasting fresh.

q: Which food element most reliably softens the perception of tannin?
exp: Tannin binds with protein, which is why a rare steak makes a young tannic red seem rounder. Fat coats the palate and blunts the same astringency.

q: Salt in a dish does what to a wine's perceived tannin and fruit?
accept: tames tannin and brings out fruit
exp: Salt is the most reliably wine-friendly thing on a plate: it suppresses bitterness and astringency and makes fruit read more clearly.

q: Why is a high-alcohol wine a poor partner for a very spicy dish?
opts: Alcohol amplifies the burn of capsaicin
Alcohol has no effect on heat
Alcohol numbs the palate before the chilli registers
Alcohol coats the palate the way dairy fat does
exp: Ethanol and capsaicin both stimulate the same heat receptors, so each intensifies the other. Lower alcohol and a little sugar are the way out. Alcohol neither numbs the palate nor coats it: it is the casein and fat in dairy that bind capsaicin and carry it off.

q: Bitterness in the food and bitterness in the wine combine in what way?
exp: Unlike salt or acid, bitterness does not cancel. Two bitter elements compound, which is why radicchio or charred greens punish a tannic red.

q: Umami in a dish, with no salt to balance it, tends to do what to a red wine's tannin?
accept: makes it seem harder and more bitter
ans: Makes it seem harder and more bitter
exp: Glutamates push tannin toward bitterness and metal. Adding salt to the dish is often the quickest repair to a pairing failing this way.

q: Identified in Japan and associated with glutamates, which taste makes wine pairing hardest?
exp: Umami is the savoury depth in mushroom, aged cheese, cured fish, tomato and stock. It is the least wine-friendly of the basic tastes.
